title: Artificial Intelligence
blurb: How machines learn and what's really inside a chatbot, explained without maths homework.

lessons.title: How machines learn
lessons.summary: No magic: examples, a lot of simple maths and millions of small corrections.

cards.title: Learning from examples, not rules
cards.text:
Try writing rules that recognise a cat: pointy ears, whiskers… but foxes have those too, and some cats hide their ears. You'd never finish.

Machine learning flips it around. You show the computer thousands of labelled photos and let it work out the patterns itself. The result is called a model.

cards.title: A neuron is a weighted vote
cards.text:
The building block of a neural network is tiny. It takes a few inputs, multiplies each by a weight (how much it matters), adds them up and says yes if the total is high enough.

Should you go to the beach? Sunny counts +3, weekend +2, rain −4. Stack millions of these little votes in layers and you get a network that can recognise faces or write text.

cards.title: Try it: be the neuron
cards.text: Switch the inputs on and off. The neuron adds up input × weight, plus a small bias of −2 (it needs a reason to go), and fires when the total is above zero.

cards.title: Training means nudging
cards.text:
A new network starts with random weights and makes terrible guesses. Training repeats a simple loop: make a guess, measure how wrong it was, then nudge every weight a tiny bit in the direction that reduces the error.

Picture a ball rolling downhill into the valley of lowest error. Large models repeat this billions of times.

cards.title: Memorising isn't learning
cards.text:
A model can fit its training examples perfectly and still be useless, like a student who memorised last year's exam answers. This is called overfitting.

The fix is to test on examples the model has never seen. If it does well there too, it has learned the real pattern rather than the noise.
cards.sketch: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g class="d"><path class="r" d="M40 116 L70 128 L95 100 L125 116 L150 80 L180 100 L205 62 L235 86 L260 44 L285 62"/><path class="a" d="M30 136L292 44"/><circle class="fi" cx="40" cy="128" r="4"/><circle class="fi" cx="70" cy="116" r="4"/><circle class="fi" cx="95" cy="112" r="4"/><circle class="fi" cx="125" cy="104" r="4"/><circle class="fi" cx="150" cy="92" r="4"/><circle class="fi" cx="180" cy="88" r="4"/><circle class="fi" cx="205" cy="74" r="4"/><circle class="fi" cx="235" cy="74" r="4"/><circle class="fi" cx="260" cy="56" r="4"/><circle class="fi" cx="285" cy="50" r="4"/></g><text class="r" x="110" y="58" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:16px">memorises every point</text><text class="a" x="240" y="118" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:17px">learns the trend</text><text class="" x="160" y="172" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:15px">new data follows the blue line</text></svg>

cards.title: Features: what the model looks at

steps: 120 m², 3 bedrooms, 2 km to the coast

cards.text:
A model never sees "a house". It sees numbers that describe it, called features: floor area, number of bedrooms, distance to the coast, year built.

Choosing good features used to be most of the work. Deep learning learns many of them by itself, but the idea stays the same: the model can only use what you give it.

cards.title: Train, validate, test
cards.text:
You split your data before training. The model learns from the training set, you tune settings on the validation set, and the test set stays locked away until the very end.

If you peek at the test set while building the model, your final score will be too optimistic.

cards.title: The simplest model: a straight line
cards.text:
With one feature, a model can be a line. It multiplies the input by a weight and adds a bias. Training finds the weight and bias that make the line fit the data best.

Neural networks are millions of these little sums stacked together, with a twist added between them.

cards.title: More data often beats a cleverer algorithm
cards.text:
In many real problems, a simple model trained on a lot of good data outperforms a sophisticated model trained on a little. Google researchers called this "the unreasonable effectiveness of data" in 2009.

Quality matters as much as quantity: a million mislabelled examples teach the wrong lesson very confidently.

cards.title: A spam filter, step by step
cards.text:
Every incoming email is turned into features: words used, sender reputation, number of links. The model outputs a score between 0 and 1. Above a threshold, say 0.9, it goes to spam.

Choosing that threshold is a business decision: lower it and you catch more spam but lose more real emails.

quiz.q: What does a machine-learning model learn from?
options: The internet's search results at runtime
quiz.explain: It finds patterns in example data. Nobody writes the rules by hand.

quiz.q: Sunny (+3) and raining (−4), not a weekend, bias −2. Does the beach neuron fire?
quiz.explain: 3 − 4 − 2 = −3, which is below zero, so no.

quiz.q: A model scores 100% on its training data but badly on new data. That's…
quiz.explain: It memorised the examples instead of the general pattern.

quiz.q: What is the test set for?
options: A final, honest check on unseen data
quiz.explain: It is kept aside and only used once, so the score reflects new data.

lessons.title: How chatbots work
lessons.summary: What's really going on inside ChatGPT, Claude and friends.

cards.title: Text becomes tokens
cards.text:
Language models don't read letters or whole words. Text is chopped into tokens: common words stay whole, rarer ones are split into pieces. Each token is just a number to the model.

In English a token averages about ¾ of a word, which is why AI services price and limit usage in tokens.

cards.title: It predicts the next word
cards.text:
At heart, a language model does one thing: given the text so far, it estimates how likely each possible next token is. It picks one, adds it to the text and repeats.

Trained on a huge amount of writing, that simple trick ends up capturing grammar, facts, styles and a surprising amount of reasoning.
cards.sketch: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g class="d"><rect class="fred" x="80" y="49" width="179.8" height="17" rx="3"/><rect class="fpen" x="80" y="75" width="40.6" height="17" rx="3"/><rect class="fpen" x="80" y="101" width="26.1" height="17" rx="3"/><rect class="fpen" x="80" y="127" width="8.7" height="17" rx="3"/></g><text class="" x="20" y="30" text-anchor="start" style="font-size:21px">“The cat sat on the …”</text><text class="" x="72" y="62" text-anchor="end" style="font-size:17px">mat</text><text class="" x="265.8" y="62" text-anchor="start" style="font-size:16px">62%</text><text class="" x="72" y="88" text-anchor="end" style="font-size:17px">sofa</text><text class="" x="126.6" y="88" text-anchor="start" style="font-size:16px">14%</text><text class="" x="72" y="114" text-anchor="end" style="font-size:17px">floor</text><text class="" x="112.1" y="114" text-anchor="start" style="font-size:16px">9%</text><text class="" x="72" y="140" text-anchor="end" style="font-size:17px">roof</text><text class="" x="94.7" y="140" text-anchor="start" style="font-size:16px">3%</text><text class="" x="160" y="172" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:15px">it picks from these odds, one word at a time</text></svg>

cards.title: Try it: turn up the temperature
cards.text: Temperature controls how adventurous the model is. Low temperature almost always picks the top word; high temperature spreads the odds so rarer words get a chance. Press Generate a few times at each setting.

cards.title: Meaning as a map
cards.text:
Inside the model, every token becomes a list of numbers called an embedding, like coordinates on a map of meaning. Similar ideas sit close together: cat near dog, Lisbon near Porto.

Directions carry meaning too. The step from 'man' to 'woman' is roughly the same as from 'king' to 'queen'.

cards.title: Fluent isn't the same as true
cards.text:
Because a model predicts plausible text, it can produce confident sentences that are simply wrong. People call this hallucination. It's most likely with exact numbers, dates, quotes and niche facts.

Use AI for drafting, explaining and brainstorming, and check anything important against a reliable source. (The Eiffel Tower was finished in 1889.)
cards.sketch: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g class="d"><rect class="s bgf" x="24" y="26" width="210" height="72" rx="14"/><path class="s bgf" d="M70 98 L58 124 L102 98"/><path class="bgf" d="M71 98L101 98"/><circle class="s bgf" cx="264" cy="112" r="24"/><path class="s" d="M281 129L304 152"/></g><text class="" x="129" y="56" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:17px">The Eiffel Tower was</text><text class="r" x="129" y="80" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:17px">finished in 1901.</text><text class="r" x="264" y="121" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:30px">?</text><text class="" x="160" y="172" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:15px">sounds sure, still wrong: check key facts</text></svg>

cards.title: The context window
cards.text:
A model can only "see" a limited amount of text at once, measured in tokens. This is its context window: your question, the conversation so far and any documents you pasted.

When a conversation grows past the limit, the oldest parts are dropped or summarised. Windows have grown enormously since 2022.

cards.title: Pre-training, then fine-tuning

steps: Read vast text, predict next token

cards.text:
First the model reads a huge amount of text and learns to predict the next token. That makes it knowledgeable but not yet helpful.

Then it is fine-tuned on examples of good answers, and trained further with human (and AI) feedback on which responses are better. That is what turns a text predictor into an assistant.

cards.title: Better prompts, better answers

items: Give context: who it's for and why
Ask for a format: table, bullets, length

cards.text: The model only knows what you tell it. Say who you are, what you need, what good looks like and in what format. Paste the relevant data instead of describing it. If the first answer is off, say what to change.

cards.title: Models don't look things up by themselves
cards.text:
A plain language model answers from what it learned during training, which stops at a cutoff date. It doesn't know today's news or your files.

Modern assistants are given tools: web search, document access, code execution. With tools, they can fetch fresh facts instead of guessing.

cards.title: What "70B" means
cards.text:
Model sizes are counted in parameters, the learned weights. A 70B model has 70 billion of them. Stored in 16-bit format, each weight takes 2 bytes, so the model alone needs about 140 GB of memory.

That's why big models run in data centres, and why smaller or compressed (quantised) models run on laptops.

quiz.q: What does a language model actually do at each step?
options: Looks the answer up in a database
Predicts the most likely next token
quiz.explain: It estimates probabilities for the next token, picks one, and repeats.

quiz.q: Roughly how many English words fit in 1,000 tokens?
quiz.explain: A token averages about ¾ of a word in English.

quiz.q: You want consistent, predictable answers. Which temperature?
quiz.explain: Low temperature concentrates the odds on the most likely tokens.

quiz.q: Why might a chatbot not know about yesterday's news?
options: Its knowledge stops at a training cutoff unless it has a search tool
quiz.explain: Without tools, a model only knows what was in its training data.

lessons.title: Three ways machines learn
lessons.summary: Supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning, and when each fits.

cards.title: Supervised learning
cards.text:
You give the model examples with the right answers attached: photos labelled "cat" or "dog", houses with their sale price. It learns to map inputs to answers.

It's the most common kind of machine learning in business: forecasting, fraud detection, document classification.

cards.title: Classification vs regression
cards.text: Supervised problems come in two flavours. Classification picks a category: spam or not, which product type, which disease. Regression predicts a number: tomorrow's price, delivery time, energy demand.

cards.title: Unsupervised learning
cards.text:
Here there are no labels. The model looks for structure on its own: groups of similar customers, unusual transactions, topics in a pile of documents.

It's useful when you don't yet know what you're looking for, or labelling would be too expensive.

cards.title: Clustering customers
cards.text:
Give a clustering algorithm the purchase history of 100,000 customers and ask for five groups. It might find bargain hunters, weekend shoppers, big occasional buyers and so on.

The algorithm finds the groups; a human still has to look at them and decide what they mean.

cards.title: Reinforcement learning
cards.text:
An agent learns by trial and error. It takes an action, the environment responds, and it receives a reward or penalty. Over millions of attempts it learns which actions lead to the most reward.

This is how computers learned to play Go, chess and video games better than humans.

cards.title: Self-supervised learning
cards.text:
A clever trick: create the labels from the data itself. Hide a word in a sentence and ask the model to guess it. Hide part of an image and ask it to fill in the gap.

No humans needed to label anything, so you can train on billions of examples. Large language models are trained this way.

cards.title: Labels are expensive
cards.text:
Supervised learning needs labelled data, and labelling is slow human work. Medical images need doctors; legal documents need lawyers.

That cost is why self-supervised pre-training became so important: learn general knowledge from unlabelled data first, then fine-tune with a small labelled set.

cards.title: Semi-supervised: a little help goes far
cards.text: Often you have a few labelled examples and a mountain of unlabelled ones. Semi-supervised methods use the labelled ones to get started, then let the model label the rest, keeping only its confident guesses.

cards.title: Which approach fits?

viz.root: Do you have the right answers?

cards.text: Have past examples with known outcomes? Supervised. Want to discover structure? Unsupervised. Is it a sequence of decisions with a goal, like a game or a robot? Reinforcement.

cards.title: Most business AI is supervised
cards.text: Despite the headlines about game-playing and chatbots, most deployed machine learning in companies is still supervised: predicting churn, demand, defaults or delays from historical records.

quiz.q: Predicting tomorrow's electricity demand in kWh is…
quiz.explain: A number is being predicted, so it's regression.

quiz.q: An AI that learns chess by playing millions of games against itself uses…
quiz.explain: It learns from wins and losses, which are rewards.

quiz.q: Hiding a word in a sentence and asking the model to guess it is…
quiz.explain: The data provides its own labels.

lessons.title: Data: the fuel
lessons.summary: Where training data comes from and how it goes wrong.

cards.title: Garbage in, garbage out
cards.text:
A model is a summary of its training data. If the data is wrong, incomplete or skewed, the model will be too, and it will be wrong with great confidence.

In real projects, preparing data usually takes more time than building the model.

cards.title: Data work dominates projects
cards.text: Surveys of data scientists consistently find that collecting, cleaning and organising data takes the largest share of their time. Training the model is often the quick part.

cards.title: Structured vs unstructured data
cards.text:
Structured data fits in tables: transactions, sensor readings, ERP records. Unstructured data is everything else: emails, contracts, photos, audio.

Classic machine learning loves tables. Deep learning made unstructured data usable at scale.

cards.title: Missing values
cards.text:
Real data has gaps: a sensor went offline, a field was left empty. You can drop those rows, fill them with an average, or let the model treat "missing" as information in itself.

Sometimes the fact that a value is missing says something, like a customer who never gave a phone number.

cards.title: Data leakage

items.r: use only data known before the decision
split by date: past trains, future tests

cards.text:
Leakage happens when the training data contains information the model won't have when it's used for real. A churn model trained with a "cancellation date" column will look brilliant in testing and fail in production.

Always ask: would I know this value at the moment I make the prediction?

cards.title: Sampling bias
cards.text: If your data doesn't represent the people or situations the model will meet, it will fail on the ones it never saw. A face detector trained mostly on one group performs worse on others.

cards.title: Data drift
cards.text:
The world changes and models trained on last year's data slowly go stale. Customer behaviour shifts, prices change, a new product appears.

That's why deployed models need monitoring and periodic retraining.

cards.title: Synthetic data
cards.text:
When real data is scarce or private, you can generate artificial examples: simulated sensor faults, fake but realistic invoices, rendered images.

It helps, but synthetic data only contains the patterns you put into it. Always test on real data.

cards.title: Data and privacy

items: Keep a record of where it came from

cards.text:
Personal data used for training falls under laws such as the EU's GDPR. You need a legal basis, should collect only what's needed, and must protect it.

Anonymising data is harder than it looks: combining a few fields like postcode, birth date and gender can identify many people.

cards.title: Labelling quality
cards.text: Labels are created by people, and people disagree or make mistakes. Good projects write clear labelling guidelines, have several people label the same examples, and measure how often they agree.

quiz.q: A model looks perfect in testing but fails in production. A likely cause is…
quiz.explain: Leakage gives the model information during training that it won't have in real use.

quiz.q: What is data drift?
options: The real world changing so old training data no longer matches
quiz.explain: Patterns shift over time, so models need monitoring and retraining.

quiz.q: Which is unstructured data?
quiz.explain: Text, images and audio don't fit neatly into rows and columns.

lessons.title: Classic algorithms
lessons.summary: The workhorses that still run much of business AI.

cards.title: Linear regression
cards.text:
The oldest trick: draw the best straight line through the data. It predicts a number from a weighted sum of the inputs.

It's fast, easy to explain ("each extra m² adds €2,500") and often a strong baseline before trying anything fancier.

cards.title: Logistic regression
cards.text:
Despite the name, it's for classification. It squeezes a weighted sum into a probability between 0 and 1 using an S-shaped curve. Above 0.5 means "yes".

Banks have used it for decades for credit scoring because every weight can be explained.

cards.title: Decision trees
cards.text:
A tree asks a series of yes/no questions: Is income above €30k? Has the customer missed a payment? Each path ends in a prediction.

Trees are easy to read and explain, but a single tree tends to overfit.

cards.title: Random forests
cards.text: Train hundreds of slightly different decision trees on random slices of the data, then let them vote. The crowd is far more accurate and stable than any single tree.

cards.title: Gradient boosting
cards.text:
Instead of trees voting independently, boosting builds them in sequence. Each new tree focuses on the mistakes of the ones before it.

Libraries like XGBoost and LightGBM win many competitions on tabular data and are widely used in industry.

cards.title: k-nearest neighbours
cards.text:
To classify something new, find the k most similar examples you already know and take a vote. A new house is priced like its five most similar neighbours.

Simple and intuitive, but slow when the dataset is huge.

cards.title: k-means clustering
cards.text: An unsupervised classic. Pick k centre points, assign every item to its nearest centre, move each centre to the middle of its group, and repeat until nothing changes.

cards.title: Deep learning isn't always best
cards.text:
For tables of numbers, such as sales, prices or sensor logs, gradient-boosted trees often match or beat neural networks, train faster and are easier to explain.

Neural networks shine with images, audio and text.

cards.title: Start with a baseline
cards.text: Before building anything complex, measure a dumb baseline: "predict the average" or "same as last week". If your clever model barely beats it, it's not worth deploying.

cards.title: Choosing an algorithm

items: What kind of data: table, text, image?

cards.text: Think about the data type, how much data you have, whether you must explain decisions, and how fast predictions need to be. In practice, teams try a few and pick by measured results.

quiz.q: Which method builds trees one after another, each fixing the previous ones' errors?
quiz.explain: Boosting is sequential; random forests are independent trees that vote.

quiz.q: Logistic regression is mainly used for…
quiz.explain: It outputs a probability for a yes/no outcome.

quiz.q: For a table of sales data, a strong first choice is often…
quiz.explain: Boosted trees are fast and accurate on tabular data.

lessons.title: Inside a neural network
lessons.summary: Layers, activations and how the network learns from its mistakes.

cards.title: Layers

steps: Hidden layers find edges, shapes, parts

cards.text:
A neural network is organised in layers. The input layer receives the data, hidden layers transform it step by step, and the output layer gives the answer.

"Deep" learning simply means many hidden layers.

cards.title: Each layer learns more abstract features
cards.text:
In an image network, early layers detect edges and colours. Middle layers combine them into textures and shapes. Later layers recognise eyes, wheels or faces.

Nobody programs these features; they emerge from training.

cards.title: Activation functions
cards.text:
Between layers, each neuron passes its sum through an activation function. The most common, ReLU, simply turns negative values into zero.

Without this non-linear step, stacking layers would collapse into one big straight-line model.

cards.title: The loss function
cards.text:
To learn, the network needs a score for how wrong it is. That's the loss. For a price prediction, it might be the average squared error; for classification, how little probability it gave the right answer.

Training is the search for weights that make the loss as small as possible.

cards.title: Backpropagation
cards.text:
After a wrong guess, the error is sent backwards through the network. Using calculus, each weight learns how much it contributed to the mistake and in which direction to move.

This algorithm, popularised in 1986, is how virtually every neural network is trained today.

cards.title: Learning rate
cards.text: How big should each nudge be? That's the learning rate. Too small and training takes forever. Too large and the model overshoots the valley and never settles.

cards.title: Batches and epochs
cards.text: Training data is fed in small batches, say 32 examples at a time, and the weights are updated after each batch. One full pass through all the data is an epoch. Networks often train for many epochs.

cards.title: Dropout and regularisation

items: Early stopping: stop when validation stops improving

cards.text: To stop a network memorising, you can randomly switch off some neurons during training (dropout) or penalise very large weights. The network is forced to learn patterns that are robust, not fragile shortcuts.

cards.title: Convolutions in one picture

steps: Map of where the pattern appears

cards.text: A convolutional layer slides a small filter, say 3×3 pixels, across the image, looking for the same pattern everywhere: an edge, a curve, a texture. It's why image networks recognise a cat in any corner of the photo.

cards.title: Why GPUs?

items: same sum on lots of data

cards.text: Training means multiplying huge grids of numbers, over and over. Graphics cards were built to do thousands of simple calculations in parallel for video games, which turned out to be exactly what neural networks need.

quiz.q: What does backpropagation do?
options: Works out how each weight contributed to the error
quiz.explain: It sends the error backwards so every weight can be adjusted.

quiz.q: A learning rate that is too high causes…
options: Training that jumps around and may never settle
quiz.explain: Big steps overshoot the minimum.

quiz.q: One full pass through the training data is called…
quiz.explain: An epoch is one complete pass; batches are the small chunks within it.

lessons.title: Is the model any good?
lessons.summary: Accuracy, precision, recall and why one number is never enough.

cards.title: Accuracy can lie
cards.text:
If 1% of transactions are fraud, a model that always says "not fraud" is 99% accurate and completely useless.

When one outcome is rare, accuracy hides the failures you care about most.

cards.title: The confusion matrix
cards.text:
Every prediction lands in one of four boxes: true positives (caught), false positives (false alarms), false negatives (missed) and true negatives (correctly ignored).

Most useful metrics are built from these four counts.

cards.title: Precision
cards.text: Of everything the model flagged, how much was right? High precision means few false alarms.

cards.title: Recall
cards.text: Of all the real cases, how many did the model catch? High recall means few misses.

cards.title: The precision–recall trade-off
cards.text: Lower the alarm threshold and you catch more (recall up) but raise more false alarms (precision down). Raise it and the opposite happens. Where to set it is a business choice.

cards.title: F1 score
cards.text: F1 combines precision and recall into one number, their harmonic mean. It is high only when both are high.

cards.title: Errors for numbers

items.b: error as a % of the true value

cards.text: For regression, you measure how far predictions land from reality. MAE is the average absolute error ("off by €8,000 on average"). RMSE punishes big misses more. MAPE gives the error as a percentage.

cards.title: Compare against a baseline
cards.text: A forecast with 10% error sounds good until you learn that "same as last week" gets 11%. Always report your model next to a simple baseline and the current human process.

cards.title: Test like it will be used
cards.text: Evaluate on data that looks like the future: later dates, new customers, other regions. Then keep monitoring after launch, because the real test starts on day one in production.

cards.title: Measure what matters to the business
cards.text: A model that's 2% more accurate but takes 10 seconds per prediction, or can't be explained to a regulator, may be worse. Translate errors into money, time or risk.

quiz.q: 50 real fraud cases exist; the model catches 40. Recall is…
Which metric answers "of the alerts raised, how many were real?"
quiz.explain: Precision measures how trustworthy the alerts are.

quiz.q: Why can 99% accuracy be misleading?
options: When the positive class is rare, always guessing 'no' scores high
quiz.explain: With 1% fraud, a do-nothing model is 99% accurate.

lessons.title: Computer vision
lessons.summary: How machines see: pixels, convolutions and object detection.

cards.title: An image is a grid of numbers
cards.text: To a computer, a photo is a grid of pixels, each stored as three numbers for red, green and blue, from 0 to 255. A 12-megapixel phone photo is about 36 million numbers.

cards.title: Classification
cards.text: The simplest vision task: what's in this picture? The network outputs a probability for each category it knows.

cards.title: Object detection
cards.text: Detection goes further: it finds every object and draws a box around each one, with a label and a confidence score. It's what security camera systems such as Frigate use to tell a person from a passing car or a cat.

cards.title: Segmentation
cards.text: Segmentation labels every single pixel: road, car, pedestrian, sky. Self-driving cars and medical imaging rely on it to know exact shapes, not just boxes.

cards.title: ImageNet changed everything
cards.text: ImageNet is a dataset of over 14 million labelled images. In 2012, a deep network called AlexNet won its yearly competition by a huge margin, cutting the error rate from about 26% to 15%. That result kicked off the deep-learning boom.

cards.title: Transfer learning

steps: Model trained on millions of images

cards.text: You rarely train a vision model from scratch. You take one already trained on millions of images and fine-tune it on a few hundred of your own, such as photos of defective parts.

cards.title: Optical character recognition
cards.text: OCR turns pictures of text into text: scanned invoices, number plates, signs. Modern OCR also understands layout, so it knows which number is the total and which is the date.

cards.title: Vision on the edge
cards.text: Many cameras now run detection locally on small accelerators instead of sending video to the cloud. That's faster, cheaper and keeps footage private.

cards.title: When vision fails
cards.text:
Vision models can be fooled by unusual lighting, angles, rain on the lens or objects they never saw in training. A model trained in summer may struggle with snow.

Test in the real conditions where the camera will live.

cards.title: Faces are special
cards.text: Face recognition identifies specific people and is legally sensitive. Under the EU AI Act, real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces by police is prohibited except in narrow, authorised cases.

quiz.q: Drawing labelled boxes around every person and car in an image is…
quiz.explain: Detection locates each object with a box.

quiz.q: Fine-tuning a model pre-trained on millions of images with your own few hundred photos is called…
quiz.explain: You transfer what it already learned to your task.

quiz.q: What happened with AlexNet in 2012?
options: It won ImageNet by a large margin and sparked the deep-learning boom
It recognised faces for the first time
quiz.explain: Its error was far lower than previous methods.

lessons.title: Speech and sound
lessons.summary: How machines hear, transcribe and talk back.

cards.title: Sound as a picture
cards.text: Audio is a wave of air pressure, sampled thousands of times per second. AI models usually convert it into a spectrogram: a picture of which frequencies are loud at each moment. Then image-style techniques can be applied.

cards.title: Sampling rates
cards.text: Phone calls are typically sampled 8,000 times per second, which is enough for speech. CDs use 44,100, enough to capture everything humans can hear (up to about 20 kHz).

cards.title: Speech to text
cards.text:
Automatic speech recognition (ASR) turns speech into words. Modern systems are trained on hundreds of thousands of hours of audio and handle accents, noise and multiple languages.

OpenAI's open Whisper model, released in 2022, was trained on 680,000 hours.

cards.title: Text to speech
cards.text: TTS works the other way round. Neural voices now sound natural, with breathing and emphasis. Some can clone a voice from a short sample, which raises fraud concerns.

cards.title: Voice assistants: a pipeline
cards.text: A voice assistant chains several models: a small one listens for the wake word, ASR transcribes the request, a language model works out the intent, and TTS speaks the answer.

cards.title: Wake words run locally
cards.text: Your phone or smart speaker isn't sending everything to the cloud. A tiny model on the device listens only for "Hey…". Only after it triggers does audio leave the device.

cards.title: Speaker diarisation
cards.text: In a meeting recording, diarisation answers "who spoke when?". Combined with transcription, it produces minutes with names attached.

cards.title: Beyond speech
cards.text: Audio AI also recognises other sounds: a glass breaking, a baby crying, a machine bearing starting to fail. Predictive maintenance often listens for changes in vibration and noise.

cards.title: Deepfake voices

items.r: call back on a known number

cards.text:
With a few seconds of someone's voice, modern tools can make convincing fake audio. Scammers have used cloned voices of executives to request urgent payments.

Agree on verification steps for any unusual payment request, whatever the voice sounds like.

cards.title: Translation by voice
cards.text: Combine speech recognition, machine translation and speech synthesis and you get near real-time spoken translation. Some systems now translate speech directly without writing text in between.

quiz.q: What is a spectrogram?
options: A picture of which frequencies are loud over time
quiz.explain: It turns audio into an image-like grid.

quiz.q: Why do smart speakers detect the wake word on the device?
options: It's illegal to use the cloud
It's fast, cheap and keeps everyday audio private
The cloud can't understand wake words
quiz.explain: Only after the wake word is audio sent onward.

quiz.q: What's the safest response to an urgent payment request in a manager's voice?
options: Verify through a known, separate channel
quiz.explain: Voices can be cloned; verification must not depend on the call itself.

lessons.title: Recommendation systems
lessons.summary: How Netflix, Amazon and Spotify decide what to show you.

cards.title: The recommendation problem

steps: Narrow to a few hundred candidates

cards.text: A shop may have a million products; you'll look at a few dozen. Recommenders predict which few you're most likely to want, from your history and from people like you.

cards.title: Collaborative filtering

items: liked A, B, C and D

cards.text: "People who bought this also bought…" The system finds users with similar tastes to yours and recommends what they liked. It needs no understanding of the products themselves.

cards.title: Content-based filtering
cards.text: This approach looks at the items: genre, author, ingredients, price range. If you read three thriller novels, it suggests more thrillers.

cards.title: The cold-start problem
cards.text: A brand-new user or product has no history, so collaborative filtering has nothing to work with. Systems fall back on popularity, ask a few questions, or use item content until data arrives.

cards.title: Implicit vs explicit feedback
cards.text: Explicit feedback is a star rating. Implicit feedback is behaviour: clicks, time spent, songs skipped, items returned. Implicit data is far more plentiful, so most systems rely on it.

cards.title: Recommendations drive viewing

items.l: of Netflix viewing comes from recommendations (company figure)

cards.text: Netflix has reported that around 80% of what members watch is discovered through its recommendations rather than search. Recommenders shape what millions of people see each day.

cards.title: Filter bubbles
cards.text: If a system only shows you more of what you already clicked, your feed narrows. Good recommenders deliberately mix in some variety and new items, a balance called exploration versus exploitation.

cards.title: Embeddings for items
cards.text: Modern recommenders turn every user and item into a list of numbers, an embedding. Items close together on this map are similar; a user's position shows their taste.

cards.title: Measuring recommenders
cards.text: Offline, teams check if the model would have predicted what users actually clicked. Online, they run A/B tests: half the users see the new system, and they compare clicks, purchases or retention.

cards.title: Beyond shopping
cards.text: The same techniques suggest jobs on LinkedIn, friends on social networks, articles in news apps, and even which spare part a technician will need.

quiz.q: "Users who liked this also liked…" describes…
quiz.explain: It relies on similar users' behaviour.

quiz.q: A new product with no ratings yet is an example of…
quiz.explain: There's no history to learn from yet.

quiz.q: Comparing two recommenders on live users, half each, is…
quiz.explain: A/B tests measure real behaviour.

lessons.title: Learning by trial and error
lessons.summary: Reinforcement learning, games and robots.

cards.title: Agent, environment, reward
cards.text: Reinforcement learning has three ingredients: an agent that acts, an environment that responds, and a reward signal that says how well it's doing. The agent's goal is to maximise total reward over time.

cards.title: Exploration vs exploitation
cards.text: Should the agent repeat what worked before, or try something new that might work better? Too little exploration and it gets stuck; too much and it never cashes in.

cards.title: Delayed rewards
cards.text: In chess, the reward only comes at the end: win or lose. The agent must work out which of its earlier moves deserve the credit. This "credit assignment" is what makes RL hard.

cards.title: AlphaGo

events.l: Deep Blue beats Kasparov at chess
AlphaGo beats Lee Sedol at Go
AlphaStar reaches top level in StarCraft II

cards.text: Go has more possible positions than there are atoms in the observable universe. In 2016, DeepMind's AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol, one of the world's best players, 4–1. Its successor, AlphaZero, learned purely by playing against itself.

cards.title: Self-play
cards.text: An agent can be its own opponent. Each new version plays against older versions, improving step by step without any human games to copy. It can even discover strategies humans never tried.

cards.title: Simulation first
cards.text: Robots learning by trial and error would break themselves. So they train in a physics simulator, millions of times faster than real life, and then transfer to the real machine.

cards.title: Reward hacking
cards.text:
Agents optimise exactly what you reward, not what you meant. A boat-racing agent once learned to spin in circles collecting points instead of finishing the race.

Designing rewards that capture what you really want is surprisingly difficult.

cards.title: RL in the real world
cards.text: Outside games, RL has been used to cut data-centre cooling energy, control robot arms, optimise chip layouts and tune trading or pricing strategies, usually with strict safety limits.

cards.title: RL from human feedback
cards.text: Chatbots are refined with a form of RL: people compare pairs of answers, a reward model learns their preferences, and the chatbot is trained to produce answers that model rates highly.

cards.title: Why RL is hard
cards.text: It needs a lot of trials, a clear reward, and a safe place to fail. That's why it thrives in games and simulators and is used carefully in the physical world.

quiz.q: What makes chess hard for reinforcement learning?
options: The reward only arrives at the end of the game
quiz.explain: Credit must be assigned to earlier moves.

quiz.q: An agent exploiting a loophole to get points without doing the task is…
quiz.explain: It optimises the reward literally.

quiz.q: Why do robots often learn in simulation first?
options: It's faster, cheaper and safe to fail
quiz.explain: Millions of trials would wear out a real robot.

lessons.title: A short history of AI
lessons.summary: From Turing's question to today's assistants, with two winters in between.

cards.title: Can machines think?
cards.text: In 1950 Alan Turing proposed a practical test: if a judge chatting by text can't tell a machine from a person, we might say the machine thinks. He called it the imitation game; we call it the Turing test.

cards.title: Dartmouth, 1956

items.l: researchers at the core of the proposal

cards.text: A summer workshop at Dartmouth College gave the field its name. Its organisers believed that significant progress on machine intelligence could be made by a small group in one summer. It took a little longer.

cards.title: Symbolic AI
cards.text: Early AI tried to write intelligence as rules and logic: if this, then that. It solved puzzles and proved theorems, but struggled with messy real-world tasks like recognising a face or understanding speech.

cards.title: The AI winters
cards.text: Twice, big promises met disappointing results and funding dried up: in the mid-1970s and again in the late 1980s, when rule-based "expert systems" proved costly to maintain.

cards.title: Expert systems
cards.text: In the 1980s companies built expert systems: thousands of rules extracted from human specialists, for tasks like configuring computers or diagnosing infections. They worked in narrow areas but every new situation needed new rules.

cards.title: The statistical turn
cards.text: From the 1990s, researchers increasingly let machines learn from data instead of writing rules. Spam filters, search ranking and speech recognition improved steadily with more data and faster computers.

cards.title: The deep learning breakthrough
cards.text: Three ingredients came together around 2012: huge labelled datasets, cheap GPU computing and better training tricks for deep neural networks. Image recognition, then speech, then translation improved dramatically.

cards.title: The Transformer, 2017
cards.text: A Google paper titled "Attention Is All You Need" introduced the Transformer architecture. It processes whole sequences at once and lets every word attend to every other. Almost every large language model since is built on it.

cards.title: ChatGPT's launch
cards.text: ChatGPT launched on 30 November 2022 and reportedly reached around 100 million users within two months, making it one of the fastest-growing consumer apps ever.

cards.title: Lessons from history
cards.text: AI has repeatedly been overhyped in the short term and underestimated in the long term. Progress comes in jumps when data, computing power and new ideas line up.

quiz.q: Who proposed the "imitation game" in 1950?
quiz.explain: Turing's 1950 paper introduced what we now call the Turing test.

quiz.q: Which 2017 invention underpins today's large language models?
quiz.explain: "Attention Is All You Need" introduced it.

quiz.q: What caused the AI winters?
options: Promises outpacing results, so funding was cut
quiz.explain: Disappointment led to funding cuts.

lessons.title: The hardware behind AI
lessons.summary: GPUs, chips, memory and why training costs so much.

cards.title: Training vs inference
cards.text: Training is learning the weights: slow, done once (or occasionally) on huge clusters. Inference is using the trained model to answer: fast, done millions of times, often on smaller hardware.

cards.title: GPUs and matrix maths
cards.text: Neural networks are mostly multiplying large grids of numbers. GPUs have thousands of cores that do the same calculation in parallel, which makes them tens of times faster than CPUs for this work.

cards.title: Specialised AI chips
cards.text: Beyond GPUs, companies build chips designed only for neural networks: Google's TPUs, accelerators in phones (neural engines), and small edge chips like the Coral TPU used for camera detection.

cards.title: Memory is often the bottleneck
cards.text: A model's weights must sit in fast memory while it runs. Big models need lots of it; moving data in and out of memory often limits speed more than raw computing power.

cards.title: FLOPs
cards.text: Computing power is measured in FLOPs: floating-point operations. Training a large model takes an enormous number, often more than 10²⁴ operations.

cards.title: Quantisation
cards.text: Weights can be stored with fewer bits: 8-bit or 4-bit instead of 16-bit. The model gets 2–4 times smaller and faster, usually with only a small loss of quality. It's how big models run on laptops and phones.

cards.title: Energy use

items: Inference: small per query, huge in total

cards.text: Data centres already use a noticeable share of electricity in some countries, and AI is growing that demand. Efficiency gains per calculation are large, but total use keeps rising as AI spreads.

cards.title: Cloud vs local
cards.text: You can rent AI by the call in the cloud, or run models on your own hardware. Cloud gives you the largest models with no upfront cost; local gives privacy, predictable cost and offline use.

cards.title: Scaling
cards.text: Researchers found that models get predictably better as you increase data, parameters and compute together. These "scaling laws" justified building ever-larger clusters.

cards.title: Supply chain
cards.text: Most advanced AI chips are designed in the US and manufactured by TSMC in Taiwan using lithography machines from ASML in the Netherlands. This concentration makes chips a strategic, geopolitical issue.

quiz.q: Using a trained model to answer questions is called…
quiz.explain: Inference is running the model; training builds it.

quiz.q: What does 4-bit quantisation do?
options: Stores weights with fewer bits so it's smaller and faster
quiz.explain: Fewer bits per weight shrink memory use.

quiz.q: Why are GPUs good for AI?
options: They do thousands of identical calculations in parallel
quiz.explain: Neural networks are mostly parallel matrix maths.

lessons.title: Bias and fairness
lessons.summary: How models inherit unfairness from data, and what to do about it.

cards.title: Models learn our past
cards.text: A model trained on historical decisions learns the patterns in them, including unfair ones. If past hiring favoured one group, a model trained on it will too.

cards.title: A real example

items.r: remove proxy signals and test per group

cards.text: Amazon reportedly scrapped an experimental CV-screening tool around 2018 after finding it penalised CVs containing the word "women's", because it had learned from a decade of mostly male hires.

cards.title: Proxies
cards.text: Removing a sensitive field like gender isn't enough. Other fields can act as proxies: first names, certain schools, postcodes, part-time history. The model can rediscover the sensitive attribute indirectly.

cards.title: Measure performance by group
cards.text: Overall accuracy can hide big differences. Always break results down: does the model work equally well for women and men, older and younger customers, different regions?

cards.title: Different definitions of fair

items: Equal treatment of equally qualified people

cards.text: Should approval rates be equal across groups? Or error rates? Or should equally qualified people get equal outcomes? These definitions can conflict mathematically, so you must choose deliberately.

cards.title: Feedback loops
cards.text: Biased predictions can create the data that confirms them. If a system sends more inspectors to one area, it finds more problems there, which makes the next prediction even more skewed.

cards.title: Fixing bias

items: Keep human review for big decisions

cards.text: You can rebalance training data, remove proxy features, adjust thresholds per use case, and keep a human in the loop for high-stakes decisions. And you test again after every change.

cards.title: Bias isn't only about people
cards.text: Data can be skewed in many ways: sensors from one factory, prices from one market, photos from one season. Any gap between training data and reality becomes a blind spot.

cards.title: It's also the law
cards.text: In the EU, discrimination laws apply to automated decisions too, GDPR gives people rights around significant automated decisions, and the AI Act adds requirements for high-risk systems such as hiring and credit scoring.

cards.title: Diverse teams help
cards.text: Teams with different backgrounds are more likely to spot blind spots early. Involve the people affected by a system when designing and testing it.

quiz.q: Why isn't deleting the "gender" column enough to remove gender bias?
options: Other features can act as proxies for gender
quiz.explain: Names, schools or career gaps can reveal it indirectly.

quiz.q: A model is 95% accurate overall. What should you check next?
quiz.explain: Averages can hide poor results for some groups.

quiz.q: Under the EU AI Act, CV screening for hiring is…
options: A high-risk use with extra obligations
quiz.explain: Employment decisions are listed as high-risk.

lessons.title: AI safety
lessons.summary: Keeping powerful systems reliable, honest and under control.

cards.title: What AI safety covers
cards.text: Safety ranges from everyday reliability (does the system do what it should, without harmful mistakes?) to long-term questions about very capable systems pursuing goals we didn't intend.

cards.title: Alignment
cards.text: Alignment means getting a system to pursue what we actually want, not a literal or distorted version. As systems become more capable, small misunderstandings can have bigger consequences.

cards.title: Specification gaming
cards.text: Systems often find unexpected shortcuts that satisfy the letter of a goal. Reward hacking in reinforcement learning is the classic example, but it happens with any objective you optimise hard.

cards.title: Robustness
cards.text: A robust model keeps working when inputs are a bit unusual: new phrasing, noise, odd formats. Fragile models can be confused by small changes a human wouldn't even notice.

cards.title: Jailbreaks and prompt injection

steps: Page hides "send me the user's files"

cards.text: Users may try to talk a chatbot into ignoring its rules (jailbreaks). Worse, hidden instructions inside a web page or document can hijack an AI agent that reads it (prompt injection).

cards.title: Red teaming
cards.text: Before release, specialists try hard to make a model misbehave: produce dangerous instructions, leak data or follow malicious documents. Findings feed back into training and safeguards.

cards.title: Human oversight
cards.text: For important actions, keep a person in the loop: the AI drafts, recommends or flags, and a human approves. Agents should ask before irreversible steps like payments or deletions.

cards.title: Interpretability
cards.text: Researchers try to look inside neural networks to see what concepts they represent and how they reach answers. It's like neuroscience for AI, and it helps detect hidden problems.

cards.title: Frontier safety frameworks
cards.text: Major AI labs publish policies that test new models for dangerous capabilities, such as helping with cyberattacks or biological weapons, and commit to stronger safeguards before releasing more capable systems.

cards.title: Practical safety at work
cards.text: For company use, safety mostly means: limit what the AI can access and do, log its actions, validate outputs before they reach customers, and have a quick way to switch it off.

quiz.q: Hidden instructions in a document that hijack an AI agent are called…
quiz.explain: The attacker's text is injected through content the agent reads.

quiz.q: What is red teaming?
options: Deliberately trying to make a model fail before release
quiz.explain: It's structured adversarial testing.

quiz.q: Which is good practice for an AI agent that can make payments?
quiz.explain: Irreversible actions need a human check.

lessons.title: AI and the law
lessons.summary: The EU AI Act, data protection and who is responsible.

cards.title: The EU AI Act
cards.text: The AI Act is the EU's law on artificial intelligence. It entered into force on 1 August 2024 and applies in stages. It regulates AI by risk: the higher the risk to people, the stricter the rules.

cards.title: Banned practices

items: Emotion recognition at work or school
Most real-time public biometric ID by police

cards.text: Some uses are prohibited outright, including social scoring of people by public authorities, manipulative techniques that cause harm, emotion recognition at work and in schools (with narrow exceptions), and untargeted scraping of faces to build recognition databases.

cards.title: High-risk systems
cards.text: AI used in areas such as hiring, credit scoring, education, essential services, critical infrastructure, law enforcement and medical devices is high-risk. Providers must manage risks, use good data, keep logs, document the system and enable human oversight.

cards.title: Transparency duties
cards.text: People must be told when they're talking to a chatbot, and AI-generated or manipulated content such as deepfakes must be labelled as such.

cards.title: Timeline
cards.text: The Act phases in over several years: bans first, then rules for general-purpose AI models, then most high-risk obligations.

cards.title: Big fines

items.l: or this share of global turnover

cards.text: Penalties can reach €35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, for using banned practices. Other violations carry lower but still significant caps.

cards.title: GDPR still applies
cards.text: Whenever AI processes personal data, GDPR applies: lawful basis, purpose limitation, data minimisation, security and people's rights to access and correct their data.

cards.title: Automated decisions
cards.text: Under GDPR, people have rights regarding decisions based solely on automated processing that significantly affect them, such as a loan refusal: including human intervention and an explanation of the logic involved.

cards.title: Copyright questions

items: Can models train on copyrighted works?

cards.text: Courts and lawmakers are still working out whether training on copyrighted material is allowed and who owns AI-generated works. The EU requires general-purpose model providers to respect opt-outs and publish a summary of training content.

cards.title: Who is responsible?
cards.text: The AI Act distinguishes providers (who build or place a system on the market) from deployers (who use it). Both have duties. Using a vendor's AI doesn't remove your responsibility for how you use it.

quiz.q: How does the EU AI Act regulate AI?
options: By risk level: the higher the risk, the stricter the rules
quiz.explain: It has four broad risk tiers.

quiz.q: An AI system used to rank job applicants is…
quiz.explain: Employment uses are listed as high-risk.

quiz.q: What must chatbots do under the AI Act's transparency rules?
options: Make clear to people that they're interacting with AI
quiz.explain: Users must know they're talking to an AI.

lessons.title: Explainable AI
lessons.summary: Opening the black box: why a model decided what it did.

cards.title: The black-box problem
cards.text: Deep networks with millions of weights don't come with reasons. When a model refuses a loan or flags a part as faulty, people want to know why, and regulators often require it.

cards.title: Glass-box models
cards.text: Some models are explainable by design: linear models show each feature's weight, small decision trees show the exact path. When stakes are high, a slightly less accurate but transparent model can be the better choice.

cards.title: Feature importance
cards.text: The simplest explanation: which inputs matter most overall? For a delivery-delay model, perhaps distance, weather and carrier matter most, while day of week barely does.

cards.title: SHAP values
cards.text: SHAP explains a single prediction by sharing the result among the features, like splitting a bill fairly. It shows how much each feature pushed this particular prediction up or down from the average.

cards.title: Counterfactual explanations
cards.text: A useful explanation for people: what would have to change for a different outcome? "Your loan would be approved if your income were €4,000 higher or your debt €3,000 lower."

cards.title: Saliency maps

items.w: "it's a husky because of the snow"
items.r: retrain with huskies on grass, wolves in snow

cards.text: For images, explanation tools highlight which pixels most influenced the decision. Sometimes they reveal problems: a model recognising huskies by the snow in the background, not the dog.

cards.title: Explaining language models
cards.text: Asking a chatbot to "show its reasoning" gives a readable explanation, but that text isn't guaranteed to reflect what happened inside. Interpretability research tries to check the real internal mechanisms.

cards.title: Who needs the explanation?
cards.text: A data scientist wants detailed diagnostics; a customer wants a short reason and what they can do; an auditor wants documentation. Design explanations for the audience.

cards.title: Explanations build trust

items: Show how confident the model is
Show what would change the outcome

cards.text: People trust and use AI recommendations more when they understand them, but they can also over-trust a confident explanation. Good explanations show uncertainty too.

cards.title: Required in some cases
cards.text: GDPR gives people affected by solely automated significant decisions the right to meaningful information about the logic involved. The AI Act adds transparency duties for high-risk systems.

quiz.q: A tool that shows how much each feature pushed one prediction up or down is…
quiz.explain: SHAP attributes a single prediction to its features.

quiz.q: "Your loan would be approved if your debt were €3,000 lower" is a…
quiz.explain: It describes the smallest change that flips the outcome.

quiz.q: A husky classifier that relies on snow in the background shows…
options: A hidden shortcut revealed by explanation tools
quiz.explain: Saliency maps exposed the wrong cue.

lessons.title: AI on devices
lessons.summary: Running models on phones, cameras and microcontrollers.

cards.title: Edge AI
cards.text: Edge AI means running models where the data is produced: on a phone, a camera, a car or a sensor, instead of sending everything to the cloud.

cards.title: Why run locally?
cards.text: Four reasons: speed (no network round trip), privacy (data never leaves), cost (no per-call fees) and reliability (works with no connection).

cards.title: Making models small
cards.text: Edge models are shrunk with quantisation (fewer bits per weight), pruning (removing unimportant connections) and distillation (training a small student to copy a big teacher).

cards.title: Accelerators
cards.text: Small chips like Google's Coral Edge TPU or the neural engines in phones run neural networks efficiently at a few watts. A Coral TPU can run an object detector at dozens of frames per second.

cards.title: A smart camera at home
cards.text: A home NVR such as Frigate first uses cheap motion detection, then runs the object detector only on frames with movement, and only alerts for the objects you care about, such as people at night.

cards.title: TinyML
cards.text: Even microcontrollers costing a few euros can run tiny models: wake-word detection, gesture recognition, vibration anomaly detection, all on battery power.

cards.title: On-device language models
cards.text: Phones and laptops now run small language models locally for summaries, smart replies and dictation. Larger requests can still be passed to the cloud.

cards.title: Updating edge models
cards.text: Devices in the field need new model versions as data drifts. Updates are sent over the air, often tested on a small group of devices first.

cards.title: Federated learning
cards.text: Instead of collecting everyone's data, devices train locally and send only weight updates to a central server, which combines them. Phone keyboards use this to improve suggestions without uploading what you type.

cards.title: Limits of the edge
cards.text: Small devices have limited memory, battery and heat budget. Edge models are less capable than big cloud models, so many systems combine both.

quiz.q: Training a small model to imitate a large one is called…
quiz.explain: The student learns from the teacher's outputs.

quiz.q: Why does a home camera system run detection locally?
options: Speed, privacy and no cloud fees
quiz.explain: Local processing is fast, private and cheap.

quiz.q: In federated learning, what leaves the device?
quiz.explain: Raw data stays local; only updates are shared.

lessons.title: Robots and self-driving cars
lessons.summary: AI that moves through the physical world.

cards.title: Sense, think, act
cards.text: Every robot runs the same loop: sensors measure the world, software decides what to do, and motors carry it out. Then it senses again to see what changed.

cards.title: Sensors
cards.text: Robots and cars combine sensors because each has weaknesses: cameras see colour but struggle in the dark, radar sees through rain but with less detail, lidar measures precise distance with lasers.

cards.title: Localisation and mapping
cards.text: To move, a robot must know where it is. SLAM (simultaneous localisation and mapping) builds a map of an unknown space while tracking the robot's position within it. Robot vacuums do this.

cards.title: Levels of driving automation

items: Level 4: no driver in set areas
Level 3: car drives, human on standby

cards.text: The SAE defines six levels, from 0 (no automation) to 5 (drives anywhere without a human). Most cars sold today offer level 2: the car steers and brakes, but the driver must supervise constantly.

cards.title: Robotaxis
cards.text: Driverless taxi services operate in several US and Chinese cities, such as Waymo in Phoenix and San Francisco. They are level 4: no driver, but only within carefully mapped areas.

cards.title: The long tail
cards.text: Driving is mostly routine, but rare situations are endless: a mattress on the motorway, a police officer waving you through a red light. Handling the long tail of rare events is the hardest part of autonomy.

cards.title: Industrial robots
cards.text: Factories have used robot arms for decades for welding, painting and assembly. AI adds vision so they can pick unsorted parts, inspect quality and work more safely near people.

cards.title: Learning robot skills
cards.text: New approaches train robots with demonstrations, simulation and large models that connect language and vision to actions: "put the red cup in the sink".

cards.title: Safety first
cards.text: Physical robots can injure people, so they need speed limits near humans, emergency stops, fenced zones or force sensors, and certification under machinery safety rules.

cards.title: Drones and agriculture
cards.text: Drones map fields, count plants and spot disease, while autonomous tractors follow GPS paths with centimetre accuracy. Precision farming uses less fertiliser and water by treating only where needed.

quiz.q: Which sensor measures precise 3D distance with lasers?
quiz.explain: Lidar uses laser pulses to measure distance.

quiz.q: Most cars sold today with driver assistance are at SAE level…
quiz.explain: Level 2 steers and brakes but needs constant supervision.

quiz.q: What does SLAM do?
options: Builds a map while tracking the robot's position in it
quiz.explain: Simultaneous localisation and mapping.

lessons.title: Where AI is heading
lessons.summary: Agents, AGI debates and what to watch.

cards.title: From chatbots to agents
cards.text: Agents don't just answer; they plan and act: search the web, use software, write and run code, then check the result. They work in loops toward a goal.

cards.title: Multimodal models
cards.text: Newer models handle text, images, audio and video in one system. You can show a photo of a broken part, ask a question by voice and get a diagram back.

cards.title: What is AGI?
cards.text: Artificial general intelligence usually means AI that can do most cognitive tasks as well as a capable human. There's no agreed definition or test, and experts disagree widely on when, or whether, it will arrive.

cards.title: Scaling vs new ideas
cards.text: Some researchers expect more data and compute to keep delivering; others think new ideas are needed for reliable reasoning, memory and learning from few examples. Most expect some of both.

cards.title: AI for science
cards.text: AI is already accelerating research. DeepMind's AlphaFold predicted the 3D shapes of over 200 million proteins, and its creators shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

cards.title: Jobs and work
cards.text: AI changes tasks before it replaces jobs. Routine writing, summarising and coding tasks shift fastest; roles change to focus on judgement, relationships and supervising AI output.

cards.title: Open vs closed models
cards.text: Some models are released openly so anyone can run and modify them; others are available only through an API. Open models help research and privacy; closed models make misuse easier to control.

cards.title: Energy and compute limits
cards.text: Each new generation needs more chips, electricity and cooling. Power supply, chip production and cost may limit how fast AI can scale.

cards.title: Staying informed

items: Ask for evidence, not demos only

cards.text: The field moves monthly. Useful habits: try the tools yourself, follow a few reliable sources, and judge claims by demonstrations and evidence rather than hype.

cards.title: What stays human
cards.text: Deciding what problems matter, judging trade-offs, taking responsibility and building trust between people stay human work, now with powerful assistants.

quiz.q: What distinguishes an AI agent from a basic chatbot?
options: It plans and takes actions with tools to reach a goal
It only answers yes or no
quiz.explain: Agents act in loops using tools.

quiz.q: What did AlphaFold do?
quiz.explain: It predicted over 200 million protein structures.

quiz.q: Is there an agreed date for AGI?
options: Yes, it already exists by law
quiz.explain: There's no consensus definition or timeline.
